segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We and you are gonna start now.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Wait, that’s what I used to tell them, a long time ago. You have to go talk to the old, you know, old folks. That’s what I tell the young folks. I talked to someone that was from Alaska one time. That’s what I said, that’s what I told them. They said that’s a good idea, maybe he did. I don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As we get started, let me tell you the reason. The reason is, the kids are going to school here, and the adults. One of these days they’re gonna start listening to these good Cherokee talkings. There ain’t no telling if they’re going to advance that far learning it. And another reason, if you got kids or grandkids, one of these days we’re gonna pass on. At one point they might wanna listen to you talk. And they’ll let them listen to you talk. As we’re starting, tell me your full English name.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: John Calvin Bunch.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: ᏓᎶᏏ

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: ᏓᎶᏏ

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: ᎤᏌᎾᎵ

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: BunchᎢ.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There in Bunch, where did you grow up around?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Just there in Bunch.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There on the road to Beaver Church, what was it like there when you were a kid? What were some of the things you could do?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: What we did for work?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What you all did to play around.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We would play out in the woods, or just anywhere. Around the house and in the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many siblings did you have?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Four.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did all of you speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Uh-uh

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m gonna ask you a lot that I already know, but you tell me. What did your dad do to provide for y’all?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: What I first remember, we had a farm and a strawberry patch. We grew beans and people would come pick some. And he worked for Kansas City Southern. I guess that was first, and later, we just lived on a farm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he have cows?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, we had cows.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So that’s what helped y’all.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Most of it, yeah, and they would go to Colorado, to work, then he would go off to work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Working broomcorn there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, he would go there, too, and somewhere in Colorado. Where they had ski slopes, he would work there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when he used to drive the bus? When did he start that?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I guess, huh, early 60s.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did he drive for?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: 61 maybe, I really don’t know how long. A long time. I really don’t remember when he quit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was already up in years when I started riding the bus he was driving. If you did something wrong, he would come and do “this” [gesture] to you. Didn’t talk, he would just do this to you. He would do “this” from the front. If you was doing something wrong.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Which school, Greasy?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Greasy. Did he use to plant a garden?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What I wanna ask you next, I already know but...

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Or he would grow hay for the cows, and you know, and he would use the horses to plow the field. We had a big field. He would grow hay for the cows to eat in the wintertime.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about food to eat, he did grow a good amount?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, we had a big garden, but it wasn’t all just for us to eat. We went to the store or town. On Saturdays, we used to go.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I already know, but I’m gonna ask you - your mom was a good cook, huh?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: It was good, it was delicious.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did she also can?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: She canned different things - strawberries, beans, stuff like that, things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You all used that in the winter.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We killed pigs in the fall. We had meat all the time, all through the winter.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There was two of y’all boys. No, there was three. Your siblings.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Three others, four with me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You’re by yourself now.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, just me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All of y’all, when he killed a pig, did all of y’all help out?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, and our neighbors, too. Do you want their names, too?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, tell me.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: ᎱᎵ ᏣᏩᏳᎦ, my aunt was ᏣᏩᏳᎦ, they would come and help, they would kill hogs and we would [unclear] hogs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They gave them some of it, huh?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they use the intestines?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah they used those and used to fix those.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like those?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Some didn’t.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are you closely related to the Rosses?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We’re first cousins.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your mothers.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re sisters.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he use horses to pull the plow? Did you ever try it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No, I didn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t. You were too small back then.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, I was too small.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Food from the woods, did you all can that?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No, we didn’t can that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all didn’t can it. So y’all just ate it. What about mushrooms?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all look for it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah I’ve looked for mushrooms.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What kind did y’all find?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: The white ones they call wishi, and the ones they called slicks. And that’s all.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about what they call morels?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: And those, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They’re saying there’s a lot of them now. That’s what they’re talking about. I don’t know what kind it is. My nephew from Arkansas is bringing me some this evening is what he told me earlier. He’ll be there sometime this evening. I’m going to eat good tomorrow evening.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, really good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where’d you go to school?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I first started at Greasy, there at south Greasy, ‘til third grade. Then I went to north Greasy and from north Greasy, I just went to the Greasy school they have now. There I went to school.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Eighth grade, then I went to Cave Springs for four years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You finished there.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you left there, you went to the army, right?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Which way did they send you?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: At first I just stayed around Texas. For about three years. Then to Vietnam.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Then you went there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah I went there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Nine months. I was almost finished being in there when they sent me there, but I asked to go there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you asked?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: So, I went there for nine months, so I finished there. Then I got out after four years. I got out then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you really fight then?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I fixed airplanes back then, we just stayed at the airbase.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Could y’all hear bombs exploding?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You could hear it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They would shoot the bombs off.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Towards the base.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They were hitting where we were at. There wasn’t a lot of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all have to fix a lot of airplanes?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, our squadron had 11. And other squadrons had some, too, but we had a lot of planes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like helicopters or just those planes?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Fighter bombers.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Big ones.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They call them fighter planes. They would hang bombs from there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you do that, or did you just fix planes?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, I just fixed them. Or we just refueled them when they went somewhere and came back. And also, I worked alert if they needed to fly those planes out quickly, if they needed them somewhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all got them ready.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We got them ready quickly, to fly off a second time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, some of them didn’t come back sometimes.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Huh-uh. I was the only one that was crew chief. I was the only one that watched that plane. They gave me a pilot driver, a flyer, I had that. One time, just next door, there were different revetments with planes in them. He got in one of them and left. That one didn’t come back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all were friends.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They really knew him over there. All the pilots were good back then. They were nice.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when you got out of the Army? What did you do?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: For a little while, I didn’t do anything. Then I started working in Arkansas. Then, after a year, I went back to school. I went to Okmulgee then. Then I moved and started back working over there in Arkansas. Then I went to Tulsa, working in construction. And I did that for a long time, construction work. ‘81, ‘83, it was ‘83 I started working right there at the hospital.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You retired from there.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, there. I retired from there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did you work?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: 33 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I worked the same, about the same amount of time for Cherokee Nation, 33 years.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: 32 or 33, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you get to know a lot of people when you were working there, coming there? Did y’all talk in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, sometimes they would come get me to translate, or the ones that didn’t speak English that were sick, I was translating that. Me and John Ross, he was doing the same thing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then, when you were growing up, did y’all have electricity?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about water?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not at first, but I don’t remember, I was little, when they had electricity put in. But we didn’t have water. We had a refrigerator, but I was little, though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about, do you remember when you first got a TV?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: TV in English.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I don’t know what year that was going, must’ve been about….

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you think about it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I think it was about ‘60. That Jess Vann had one, he was the only one that had one. A lot of us neighbors went over there, to watch it there. We’d go over there at nighttime.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What would you watch?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They used to like to watch wrestling.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what a lot of them say, wrestling they would say.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I guess they mostly watched that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They believed it was real, huh. Me, one time, do you remember, in Ft. Smith they used to have wrestling? We went there one time, do you remember the tag team they called Assassins they had? They were wrestling.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Were they the ones who had the masks?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Masks, yeah. Those were the ones wrestling, they were wrestling someone else. There across, there was someone, and he was talking rough to them. They would argue with him, he was getting on to them and doing “this” [gesture] After a while, they went over, and he ran this way, and they chased him towards us. When he ran close by, it was my half-brother Johnny Sanders. They were chasing him. And when we talked to him, he said it was made up.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: He got away from them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He got away from them. When you think about growing up now, what was the most important thing that you miss of the past?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I think it was because we were close families. We were close to our neighbors.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all visited each other.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they talked, those adults, what did y’all do?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: When grownups talk, we weren’t allowed to listen. “Go play somewhere,” they would say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So did they say, “Don’t be hollering around, a ghost is gonna get in on it,” they would tell you.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: At night.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they had that old field at Greasy, have you ever been there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you ever play there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Albert and them lived there, they were my cousins.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I used to spend the night there sometimes, Fay and Ray, we were the same age. How about for water? Did y’all have a well?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who dug it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: The last time, different people dug it. They say, because it was solid rock.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They took it out.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, it was about four feet it was dirt, and the rest of it was solid rock. It was 15 feet, and the last time it was Joe Vann, I think. It was last one digging and he found water. It was Soldier Vann’s dad, that one. My dad’s mom and him were siblings.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, so you are related to the Vanns, too?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We’re close related.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And also, is Doris’s parents your close relatives?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not that close.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But you are related.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: But we’re related. Jesse Vann was the name of my dad’s grandpa. It was James Vann’s dad’s brother I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, how many kids do you have?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Three of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does any of them say anything in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they understand, though?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Very little.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A little bit like mine, they don’t understand anything. Do you still go to New Baptist Church?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, but last night I went to Dexter’s place.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In town?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh, they don’t have church on Wednesday there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They don’t?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: New Baptist.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We started back.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Y’all started back?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How’s Teddy doing?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I haven’t heard anything, I didn’t go there Sunday, Sunday night. I don’t know, but they didn’t say anything.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were growing up, when y’all got sick, would y’all go to the doctor, or did someone know some medicine from the woods?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We mostly went to the doctor, but we did use medicines that they knew from the woods. They knew a little medicine. We used stuff like that, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like if someone catches a cold.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Or a cold or something, or a fever. Just for things that they knew themselves, we used medicine from the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We’re gonna back up a little bit. Those pigs and cows you said he had, did y’all ever kill a cow yourself?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not a cow.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t. You could say that was work, huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mostly did y’all kill just one hog or more?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Three, two it’s all we killed, I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your dad raise the corn he fed those?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: At first he did. He grew corn, he would put them in the corn crib, for like feeding the pigs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you all use your hands to pull the corn out?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah ourselves, us children, we would pull them out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they dry, did it make your hands hurt?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: A little bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “Boy, it’s making me hurt,” I would be saying. I’d be sitting somewhere in the shade.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: While we were home by ourselves and the corn was growing, we would hoe the corn. The grown-ups would be in town, and we would be working in the field.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you all helped out that much?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all eat some of them?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, that [unclear] garden.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, he planted different places?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, different places.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you ever just ate them raw, the corn?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: One time me and Doris went to Fayetteville. We were coming back through Farmington, and there was a sign that said ‘fresh corn’, so we stopped. When I jumped, that woman was eating corn, raw. She was really eating it. That’s no [unclear] is it?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I think so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: [unclear]?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I think not.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don’t think so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She was eating that. “I don’t see how you can eat that,” I said to her. “It’s good. Try it,” she told me.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Those June corn, they call them, or sweet corn that [whites] call it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This, she called it peaches and cream.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She told me to try it. She handed it to me. I took a bite, and man, it was really good. I didn’t give it back, I ate it up.
[laugh]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “You like it?” she told me. “Yeah,” I told her. “Go ahead and eat it,” she told me.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I’ve never ate a full one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But you’ve tried it, though. If you ever hear that it’s peaches and cream, try it. Now that’s good.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Now that sweet corn I’m telling you about, now that’s kinda sweet.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you’ve ate a little of that?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: So yeah, I’ve tried it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I got it from -

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: So you took it from her?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So I took it from her. When y’all grew things like that, did your mom can it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Preserved it. What about things from the woods?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Huh, no, not that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Wild onions, things like that, she didn’t preserve that.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not wild onions though. But after a while, she froze it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, she put it in the freezer.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not long time ago, she didn’t can that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s pretty good even if it’s been in the freezer.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah it’s pretty good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s how Doris does them. That poke salad she does the same way. Yesterday she said, “I’m not gonna can as much, because we don’t eat as much.” So, I said, “Really? But you keep buying, and you still have stuff.”

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: If there some elders living somewhere, she can give them that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, they would appreciate it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Or Jimmy?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No telling. He likes that jelly. He won’t eat without jelly. But his wife makes him jelly.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Now, that elderberry jelly, is that good?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Doris makes it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She picks it at the edge of the field by the house. She makes it. When people find out, she’ll sell it all quickly.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s because they say it’s medicine.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Tell me when she has some.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Because they say it helps your immune system.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: It grows close to my house, that stuff.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tell me exactly where it’s at, I’ll go get it and she’ll make it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: OK, uh-huh, good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She makes all kinds of things into jelly. Do you know those dandelions? She makes that kind of jelly.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now that ᎤᏓ. ᏎᎷ ᎤᏓ. Corncob. She makes it from that, too.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I’ve never heard of that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, she makes things like that.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Watermelon, ᎬᎩᏍᏗ, she likes that kind.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really? Boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Here lately, I found a lot of wild grapes.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Those are about half-pint in size. She made 58 of those, jelly she made.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She really makes things.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Well I’m gonna buy from her this summer.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When she makes it, we’ll bring it to you.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh, OK, good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The elderberry you said?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Just all those things I’d like to try, corncob you said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah corncob. That preacher from Kenwood is always asking for some, but we haven’t took him any yet.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh yeah? Where do y’all get corncobs?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She gets them at Walmart, or those that came from Webber’s Falls. When she shaves those, that what she uses.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: So she actually uses the corn cobs?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really? I’ve never heard of that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She soaks them, she boils them, until they get kind of sticky. Then she mixes things in there, and it makes that jelly. She will try anything.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That’s the way they say Roger’s granddaughter was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The one that lived near Bunch?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That old woman that lived by Breedon.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That one used to tell us she made a lot of different pies a long time ago. That persimmon, like that, too. She would make that kind.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what I do, I look for things and I give it to her, to make things. When you were in the Army in Vietnam, did you ride a plane?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did it take you to go there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: 16 hours, I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you all land somewhere for a little while?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: When we first left, we left from Seattle. I got on the plane in Dallas to Seattle. We left for Japan, but we didn’t have enough fuel, so we stopped in Alaska, then we got to Japan and then to Cam Ranh base in Vietnam.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Had you been in a plane before or was that your first time?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No, I’d been in one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did it seem scary to you?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No. Those little planes, I rode in one like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about those fighters, have you ever been in one of them?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I didn’t get in one of those but when I first got there, we had what they call a TF plane. It had two seats on it. One for the front and one for the back. When I first got there, there was a crew chief that used to ride in there. And they stopped because they said other planes were going too close. They might get shot down, so they quit doing that. It was just about time for me to come back, and they started doing that again. One boy from our squadron rode in there. He went on a mission, escort on C-130. He looked like a little boy, that one that rode.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he come back?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, he came back. If I stayed a little longer and if I talked to someone about it, I could’ve rode in one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you yourself want to ride in one?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I would’ve rode one if they told me to.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, it was good that you didn’t have to see anyone get killed.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: When they attacked, some were wounded and some got killed coming in because they were wanting to destroy the planes. Those coming in did get killed. Sometimes they heard them but I didn’t, the bombs going by. One time, I was there early and we heard just at daylight it was, they heard the bomb go by. There was a church just right over there, where Vietnamese women worked, where people worked. The Vietnamese, they were working there at a base, they would be cleaning or doing different things. They killed some woman over there with that bomb. Sometimes they would just hit everywhere. One time, there was a pretty good-sized post office we had. It was kind of like a little town we had there, and streets. One time, when I first got there, we didn’t stop, we worked every day. I’d been there a while, and we got a day, we got time off. One time, I was walking, headed to the post office, the hobby shop, they called it, they had little things to play games, …. I was walking just right there, and a bomb went off just there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where you were walking?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I was walking this way, and it just hit over there. [gesture] It wasn’t real close, but I just turned and walked back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they wanting to destroy the landing strip?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: This one, they were just trying to destroy whatever. They came in at nighttime, and they were trying to destroy the planes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they walking in on foot?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, on foot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y’all had some fighting soldiers?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: We lived on this side, on the side the runway was, and the other side was the army. And where we was, behind us was the Koreans. We lived a little bit in the middle. When I first got there, 101st Airborne, they were there, across where the runway was. About that time, they moved and some different ones came.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they fight the ones that came in?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They were coming in a different end, I guess they were coming in. I guess it was just those NVC that killed them. Sometimes they would see them when they went and looked for them, and they would fight. They would go in the ground, they were thinking, when they would go look for them to fight.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what they would say, they would go into the ground.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Sappers, that’s what they called them. It’s hard to tell if they’re around. They mostly move at night time. They’d be wearing black. I guess things like that… it stays in your mind, things like that, and back then, I lived in the barracks. I lived on the second floor, that’s where I slept. I had a dream one time, and there was like a balcony on this side. They said we got overrun in the dream. I went out and I looked down, and those that wear hats were coming up the hill, and we didn’t have any guns or anything. I turned around and there was a hallway, so I took off running. I took off running, and I got shot in the back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you were just dreaming?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Sometime later, when I got back, I had that same dream. It was all the same.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y’all didn’t have any guns, so y’all couldn’t protect yourselves?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not until we got ran, then they would give us guns. But we didn’t get overrun. It was in 1969 when I got there. In February of ‘68, that was the most-hit airbase.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where you were, Phan Rang, huh?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, Phan Rang Airbase was the name. Back then, when it was February, lots of planes got bombed. Before I got there, their planes were destroyed. It was metal like this [gestures] about this thick, about eight feet, and it had dirt in it all the way around it, this way and that way and this way where the planes were. They hit one plane we had there. It’s like that metal melted all the way around. They were thick metal, they weren’t thin. It was amazing the bombs didn’t go off, because they had bombs hanging on there. It was waiting on the planes to fly, and it had guns and ammo in there. And there were also bombs laying on the side.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And they didn’t blow up?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Huh-uh, before they blew up, they put it out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was dangerous that happened.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Boy, it was dangerous. We’d be there sometimes when they would attack, and one time there was a commander, he was going to fly out when we got attacked. “Let’s go sit over there.” We sat over on the edge while they attacked. Sometimes, when we would get attacked, I would climb up that fence, and I would be up there looking around. They would be hitting in the middle.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’d be looking for a hole. But I guess if it was meant to be, it wouldn’t matter where you’re at, it’s going to happen. Were you happy when you finished there?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: For a little while I wanted to extend six months, but I didn’t do it. I was really thinking at first, I was going to be in there another four years. And over here on the stateside, it was like a regular job. All you have to do is be working, and when you are done you can go back to the barracks. Or, if you want to go to town, just go out the gate, as long as you got back to work by five. That’s the way it was. They weren’t really strict, though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you kind of could do whatever you wanted as long as you came back to work.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: As long as you came back to work. But if you got a little rank and became sergeant, you could go wherever you wanted. I mean, it didn’t have no limit. You could go everywhere. But below that, you could only go a hundred and fifty miles.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But a hundred and fifty miles is a long way.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah it was about a hundred and fifty miles to Sherman–Denison. Do you know where that is?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I was living there it was about a hundred and fifty miles to my house. Yeah, I used to come home if I wanted to, on the weekend. I would come back, yeah, that happened good for me.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What about when you were in Vietnam? What would you say was the closest town that way?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: There was a little town just on the outside, but we couldn’t go there. About the time I got there, they closed it, and they made it so you could not even go to town.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What province would you say that was?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: It was like a – I don’t remember which province it was, but it was like forty miles from Cam Ranh.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Cam Ranh.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: But on the other side was Saigon. That was still on the other side of where we were staying, towards the north.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How far were you from the real fighting? From where you were at?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They were fighting everywhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Everywhere?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: There was no front line.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: They would just stick their head out everywhere, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: What they called gunships were helpful to us. They had some like that there. I don’t know if y’all have heard of those – Puff the Dragon C-47, that is an old plane. They still use them today. That is a real safe airplane, that one was, and a C-47 had Gatling guns on it. And that thing will fire about 10,000 rounds per minute. Yeah, those things would be flying around the base at nighttime. Or a C-130. Those kinds would be flying around. If you were outside, they would shoot somewhere, and you could see a long flame. It would be red all the way to the ground.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They’d be just shooting.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, you would hear them shooting them guns. Yeah, they were watching us, they were flying around. That’s why they didn’t really bother.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were watching all the time. Did you ever really think a lot, when you weren’t doing anything, like, this could happen?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Nope.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess something like that would happen if you thought about it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, if you were thinking about things like that. I didn’t care.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And what about now, what do you do?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Not really anything around the house. I still have cows. I’m still feeding cows now. I do things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many do you own?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: 30… 20… one calf was born yesterday. There’s six calves now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They’re giving a high price for them now.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: About 28 now, if you count the calves. And the grown ones, I just keep about 28.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I went to the Stilwell sale yesterday. They sold one pair for $2,000.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: One time, when I still lived on the mountain where Mom and Dad used to live, that one cow had a calf. She would not take it. She would not let it suck. I fed it myself with milk replacer. I used that and fed it for only about two days ‘cause it was little. This boy I know was working near Watts. That’s all they do when they buy those young calves. He came and said, “Do you want to sell it?” So I said, “I will sell it.” He took a picture of it and sent it to that boss. He gave me $500 for it. Yeah, about two or three days old, he gave me $500 for it. They really were worth a lot then. Same thing happened to Dickie Harris, but he kept it for about four days. He just took it to the Stilwell sale barn and got $450 for that one. That was the most they paid for cows that size.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The other day, me and my grandchild went to the Stilwell sale. For 500-600 pounds they were paying $1,800 to $2,000. Boy, that was high.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I have a bull that’s about this [gestures] tall. He was too little to sell, so I didn’t sell him, the other calf. I have a heifer, too. Two little ones and a heifer, and it might be best if I just loaded them up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They are paying really good for them now. I was wanting to buy some, I was planning on buying some in May. I don’t know if I’m going to do it now.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Do you have a pasture?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just behind the house, but in about a week from Saturday, they’re going to clear off a little bit more.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: You need to plant rye grass and fescue, and you don’t need to plant it now, but Bermuda grass, plant that. That seed is small, it don’t take very much. It’ll spread by itself.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Not this weekend, but a week from Saturday, they’re going to clear it up. Linda’s husband, Glen Wilson that one, he’s going to lease a bulldozer.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That’s good, so he’s going to lease it? How big?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The most will be about 40 acres.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: They’re going to clear that much?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m going to try.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That’s quite a bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Really, it’s 60 acres, but there’s big trees.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Just leave those. That’s good, what about Cherokee Nation, do they have that kind of stuff?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Right there close to where we live, there’s 260 acres.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Like equipment?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh! No.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Next time that comes up to lease, I’m going to try and get it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: How much was it the last time?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Well, the last time I got it, it was $3000. And then when we let it go, me and an old man were helping each other with it, close to the house, it was ‘68 then. And now they’re talking about it being over $7000.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: How many acres?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: 200 acres, was a lot of it clear?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, yes, this past week they baled a little bit of hay on it. You can bale hay on all of it if you clean it up good.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh, that whole 260 acres?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No not all of it, but most of it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Do you know how much is clear?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, I can’t tell you it’s this many acres. Marty Horn had it, and now Jim’s stepson, that’s who has it now.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Jim who?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Doris’s brother, Jim Vann, it’s his stepson, he has it.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Oh really? OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But he don’t feed them, when they’re being fed, Jim feeds them. All right, and now, us Cherokees that have these beliefs in ghosts (Sgili), have you ever experienced anything like that?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I’m not a ghost (Sgili). No, I haven’t hardly seen anything.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you ever heard people talking about it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, we’ve been experiencing that kind of stuff for a long time. I guess it was worse a long time ago. I don’t guess it’s that bad these days.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ain’t it? I guess just the beginners are probably trying it out, I think. What about the little people?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: I’ve never seen one, but I believe in them. And also that Sasquatch, too, I believe are living.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you believe?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Those big people.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is there something? Have you seen something?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Huh-uh, no, I haven’t seen anything. I haven’t seen those little people either, but I believe in them. And the big ones, too. Tsayug said that a long time ago, a long time ago, those things hung around the Indians, that kind. That kind came up and was wanting a woman. That kind came again. “You’re going to have to get some wood, you have to do things like that,” then he turned around, I guess they’re talking Cherokee, he was telling it. And then he turned around and he went over there and pulled up a big old tree and said, “Here!” That’s what Tsayug was telling. [unintelligible/ people laughing over each other] I guess he believed it, because he kept telling it. Tsayug used to be Hul’s wife. That’s who was talking about that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The people from Belfonte, they really believe in that.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: The big ones?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, the Eagle boy, I think his name is Jimmy, do you know where the Ryder Daugherty Bridge is? He was walking there, and he heard something over there. He said he looked over there and he could see something big standing there. He said, “It was looking at me with red eyes. I didn’t run, I just walked fast. As I was leaving, it followed me. A ways away, there’s a crossing like this [gestures]. I went straight towards Nicut by the store. And it went on the other turn-off, this [gestures] way,” he was saying.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: He was coming this [gestures] way?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah. Yeah, they really believe, and also the people from Jay, they really believe.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: And also they said they saw one somewhere in Peavine. I’m not going to tell who it is, but a woman was telling me, when they were walking in the middle of the night they put a light out in the middle of the field. It was standing there, like crouched down, then he stood up and turned around. After a few days they saw him again, further down. That’s what she was saying, she was telling me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you ever heard where they beat the tree? That’s what they say, that they beat a tree with a stick really hard. I’ve heard that before.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Really? Somebody that I used to know said that he seen it, too. North of Tahlequah, back there, I’m not sure where at. He was standing by the highway, where there was stop signs. He was as tall as one of the signs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oooooh!

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That’s what he said. They said that they sound like a wolf. He was telling me that they sound a little different, he was telling me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Really, the first time I heard it, I was waiting on the wild pigs. We would spread corn around, and it happened behind me four times. It made a loud sound, and it didn’t even bother me. I didn’t think about it until I got home. They say that that’s what they do. I didn’t trap pigs anymore. We’re finishing up now. Whenever they put the Cherokees out from Georgia and North Carolina, did anybody ever mention that to you? Were any of your parents or grandparents involved in that?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: No, they never did talk about that. Didn’t Ned Bird come around that time?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That’s all I know that they talked about.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too, I heard it, too.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: That’s all I’ve heard, I’ve never heard anything else.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m going to ask you this last thing, the way we talk Cherokee now, what do you think is going to happen?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: It’s our own fault, even if our relatives talk Cherokee, they didn’t talk Cherokee to them. But I think they’ll be able to talk a little bit, but it’s going to come to an end on earth. But there’ll still be some who are speaking.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s getting close, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it, I think so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I think me and my wife fall short, we’re always talking to ourselves in Cherokee all the time. We have nine- and seven-year-old girls, that we’ve been given that we’re raising. We’ve never said, “Say this in Cherokee.” We’ve never said that to them. We’ve never tried, and that’s where we’ve come up short. If you really want to be fluent, they need to listen to how we’re talking all the time, they need to try. That’s where we come up short.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: What they’re teaching them is put different.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Put it different. Appreciate you coming, John.

segments.speaker: john-bunch
segments.translation: Me too, I’m happy.
